A service you cannot see inside is a service you cannot operate. Rust's answer is tracing for structured events, metrics/prometheus for numbers, and OpenTelemetry for distributed traces.

Why tracing, not log

log gives you a string. tracing gives you an event with fields and a span context:

Structured fields are what let you query "p99 latency by user_id" without regex-parsing logs.

Setup

RUST_LOG filters by target (module path) and level. my_app::db=trace,info means "trace for that module, info for everything else".

JSON output in production

One JSON object per line — what Loki, Elasticsearch and CloudWatch expect.

Levels

Level Use for
error something failed and a human must look
warn degraded but handled (retry, fallback, slow query)
info lifecycle events: started, connected, job finished
debug diagnostic detail, off in production
trace per-item detail, almost never on

Rule of thumb: if it fires per request, it is debug, not info. A service logging info! per request produces gigabytes a day and buries the events that matter.

Spans

A span is a unit of work with a start, an end, and fields. Events inside a span inherit its context.

#[instrument] creates a span named after the function, records each argument as a field (use skip for anything not Debug or too large), and records the returned Err at ERROR level with the error's Display.

Manual spans:

Gotcha: span.enter() returns a guard tied to the thread, not the task. In async code, holding it across an .await attributes the wrong events when the task migrates threads. Use .instrument(span) instead — it is correct by construction.

Metrics with metrics + Prometheus

The four golden signals

Signal Metric
Latency histogram of request duration
Traffic counter of requests
Errors counter of responses by status
Saturation gauge of queue depth, pool usage, memory

If you instrument only four things, instrument these.

Naming conventions

Never put an unbounded value (user id, request id, raw URL) in a label. That creates one time series per user and kills the metrics backend.

Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry

Now every #[instrument] span becomes a span in Jaeger/Tempo/Honeycomb, and tracing propagates the trace context over HTTP if you add the header propagation layer.

Health and readiness endpoints

The distinction matters: a failing liveness probe restarts the pod; a failing readiness probe only removes it from the load balancer. Getting these backwards causes restart storms.

Everything you need to correlate, filter and alert on.

Checklist for a new service

  • tracing_subscriber initialised once, at startup, before anything else
  • RUST_LOG respected; default info
  • JSON output when LOG_FORMAT=json
  • #[instrument] on every handler and every DB/HTTP call boundary
  • /healthz (liveness) and /readyz (readiness)
  • /metrics with the four golden signals
  • Request-id propagation into logs and outbound calls
  • Panic hook that logs at error
  • No println! anywhere in library code (clippy print_stdout)

Exercises

  1. Replace every println! in a small service with tracing::info! and add an EnvFilter that turns on debug only for your crate.
  2. Add #[instrument] to a handler with one field skipped, and confirm the field appears in the JSON output.
  3. Expose /metrics with a request counter and a latency histogram; scrape it with curl.
  4. Add /healthz and /readyz, with readiness checking the database.
  5. Explain why span.enter() across an .await is a bug and show the .instrument() fix.
  6. Name three label values you must never use in a Prometheus metric, and why.
